units.t: Artificial Intelligence. Episode one.
In this episode: A short history of AI, Expert systems: when AI ran on rules, How machines learn and How AI learns: walking downhill in the fog.
Part one. A short history of AI.
AI did not arrive overnight.
It is a 70-year story of bold promises, bitter winters and a few moments that stunned the world.
Turing and Dartmouth.
In 1950 the British mathematician Alan Turing, famous for wartime code-breaking, published 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', asking: can machines think?
Because 'thinking' is hard to define, he proposed the imitation game, now the Turing test.
If a judge chatting through text could not reliably tell a machine from a person, we should take its intelligence seriously.
He also predicted machines might one day learn, not just be programmed step by step.

The term 'artificial intelligence' was coined by John McCarthy in a proposal for a 1956 summer workshop at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire, organised with Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon and Nathaniel Rochester.
It produced no single breakthrough, but gave the field a name, a community and an ambitious agenda.
Early optimism.
The first decades of AI were dominated by symbolic AI: programs built from hand-written rules and logic.
They proved maths theorems, played draughts and solved puzzles.
In 1966 Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA mimicked a therapist using simple pattern matching, and some users became emotionally attached to it, which alarmed its creator.
Confidence ran high.
In 1965 Herbert Simon predicted that within twenty years machines would be capable of doing any work a person can do.
Meanwhile, Frank Rosenblatt's 1958 perceptron, an early learning machine loosely inspired by brain cells, hinted at a different path that was largely sidelined for years.
The AI winters.
Real-world problems proved far messier than puzzles.
Programs that worked in tidy demonstrations failed on everyday language and vision, and computers were too slow and data too scarce.
In the early 1970s, critical reviews such as Britain's 1973 Lighthill report led governments to cut funding, beginning the first 'AI winter'.
The 1980s brought a boom in expert systems, rule-based programs that captured specialist knowledge for businesses.
They proved expensive and brittle, and by the late 1980s and early 1990s the market collapsed into a second winter.
The lesson: hype can outrun what the technology can actually do.
Deep Blue and deep learning.
In May 1997 IBM's Deep Blue beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov 3.
5 to 2.
5 in New York, after he had beaten an earlier version the year before.
Yet it did not learn as people do.
Specialised hardware evaluated around 200 million positions per second, combined with chess knowledge programmed by experts.
It was superb at chess and could do nothing else.
Learning machines never died.
Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio kept refining neural networks through the lean years.
By the 2010s huge internet datasets, fast graphics chips, GPUs, and better training methods had arrived.
In 2012 AlexNet, from Hinton's Toronto group, won the ImageNet image-recognition competition by a striking margin.
'Deep learning' soon transformed speech, translation and image analysis.
The trio shared the 2018 Turing Award.
AlphaGo to chatbots.
Go has vastly more positions than chess, so brute force alone could not master it.
In March 2016, DeepMind's AlphaGo beat top professional Lee Sedol four games to one in Seoul.
It combined deep neural networks, search and reinforcement learning, improving partly by playing itself.
In game two it played Move 37, which experts first thought a mistake but later saw as brilliant.
Many had expected this milestone to be years away.
In 2017 Google researchers introduced the transformer, which made it practical to train on enormous amounts of text.
This led to large language models, and ChatGPT's release in November 2022 made them mainstream.
Past predictions were often wildly optimistic, yet deep learning has also surprised sceptics.
Treat confident forecasts in either direction with caution.
The key idea: In 1950 Turing proposed a conversation test of machine intelligence, and in 1956 the field was named.
